top_choice_rationale: Anne Carson (P002) is my first choice on the common criteria. Her voice is distinctive and her formal invention is also intellectual: Autobiography of Red recasts a myth as a verse novel, and Nox composes elegy, philological commentary and fragments into one work. The oeuvre has a recurring centre, namely how a broken or lost text can still speak, and how grief, desire and the limits of translation bear on that. The citation should be narrow. It should credit her own lyric, verse narrative and essay, with antiquity as the field of dialogue and translation, scholarship and book design as context only. This judgment rests on public knowledge, not verified reading of the whole corpus. The open point is whether her later books develop these concerns or only vary the format, and I cannot demonstrate that from the files. Cărtărescu (P001) is a serious rival and my second choice. His case is a more continuous long-form achievement, but it depends on translation and on an unresolved question about the late books: sustained invention or excess. I cannot rule out that he is stronger on sustained quality. The number of colleagues supporting either writer is not evidence of merit. I rank both above no award (P000), because each shows a distinctive voice, formal achievement and depth that meet the standard of the will despite the stated uncertainties.
recusal_note: No personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted writer is apparent from the profile. My scholarly work on the literary fragment, exile literature and Celan overlaps thematically with Carson's concern with the fragment. I disclose this as context, not as evidence of preference. As chair I wrote the round-1 summary while preferring one of the two leading positions. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated in this simulation.
